The man on the phone is the father, and the "hostage" whose life the kidnapper threatens is the father himself, not his daughter. The kidnapper has seized the father at his own location and is keeping him there captive while forcing the phone call; the daughter is elsewhere, desperately begging the kidnapper to spare her father's life. The kidnapper demands that 100 million yen be brought alone by noon, with no police.

The father decides the ransom should not be paid for two linked reasons. First, he believes the kidnapper will kill him regardless of whether the money is paid—the ransom would not save his life. Second, the only way the ransom could be delivered is by his daughter bringing the money alone, which would expose her to grave danger from the kidnapper. Paying would therefore gain nothing for him while endangering the person he most wants to protect.

So rather than let his daughter walk into danger to pay a ransom that will not save him, the father chooses to sacrifice his own life and refuses to have the ransom paid.

The kidnapped hostage is the father himself, not the daughter. The kidnapper is holding the father captive at his location and has put his daughter on the phone; she is desperately begging the kidnapper to spare her father's life. The kidnapper demands that 100 million yen be brought alone by noon, with no police.

The only person who could realistically bring the money on short notice is the daughter, and to do so she would have to come alone into the kidnapper's hands. The father understands that if she does this, the kidnapper will harm or kill her too—she would merely be delivering herself as a second victim. He also knows the ransom will not save his own life.

So, rather than let his daughter walk into the kidnapper's grasp to pay a ransom that cannot save him, the father tells her not to pay and accepts his own death to protect her. The ransom should not be paid because paying it would only endanger the daughter without rescuing the father.

The hostage the kidnapper threatens to kill is the father himself, not the daughter. The kidnapper is holding the father captive and has his daughter on the phone, where she is desperately begging the kidnapper to spare her father's life. The kidnapper demands that 100 million yen be brought alone by noon the next day, with no police.

The only person who could bring the money is the daughter, and doing so would mean coming alone into the kidnapper's hands—where she would be harmed or killed rather than simply making a safe delivery. The father cannot bear to let his daughter walk into that trap.

So, purely to protect his daughter from being harmed, the father tells her not to pay the ransom and refuses to have it delivered, accepting whatever happens to himself in order to keep her out of the kidnapper's grasp.

The kidnapper has not taken the daughter hostage—the threatened hostage is the father himself. He is held captive by the kidnapper, who is physically present with him and keeping him from leaving, while his daughter is elsewhere on the phone, desperately begging the kidnapper to spare her father's life. The kidnapper demands that 100 million yen be brought alone by noon the next day, with no police.

Because the father is captive and cannot deliver the money himself, the only person who could bring it is the daughter—and she would have to come alone into the kidnapper's hands. The father realizes that if she does this, the kidnapper would harm or kill her too, rather than simply take the money and release anyone; she would be walking into a trap and become a second victim. Paying the ransom would therefore endanger the very person he most wants to protect, while bringing no safety to himself.

So, primarily to keep his daughter from coming alone into the kidnapper's grasp and being harmed, the father tells her not to pay and refuses to have the ransom delivered, accepting his own fate rather than let her place herself in danger.
